tip: To introduce someone politely, Korean points at 'this side': 이쪽은 제 친구예요 (ijjogeun je chinguyeyo = this side is my friend) – softer than pointing at the person.
교사 (gyosa) is the neutral job title for your own work: 저는 교사예요 (jeoneun gyosayeyo). 선생님 (seonsaengnim) honors others – never use it for yourself.
저기요 (jeogiyo) is literally 'over there' – it's how you hail a waiter or a stranger without knowing their name.
고마워요 (gomawoyo) is warm, everyday thanks for people you know; 감사합니다 (gamsahamnida) is the formal step up for strangers and staff.
With 하다 (hada) verbs, 안 (an = not) slips between the noun and the verb: 공부 안 해요 (gongbu an haeyo) – not 안 공부해요 (an gongbuhaeyo).
English gets ON the bus; Korean rides it as a direct object: 버스를 타요 (beoseureul tayo) uses 를 (reul), no word for 'on' at all.
뭐 (mwo = what) sits right where the answer would go – no inversion: 지금 뭐 해요? (jigeum mwo haeyo?) is literally 'now what do?'
Name + 씨 (ssi) stays polite even when talking ABOUT someone, not just to them: 민수 씨가 누구예요? (Minsu ssi-ga nuguyeyo? = who is Minsu?)
Before a noun, 'what' becomes 무슨 (museun = what kind of): 무슨 요일이에요? (museun yoirieyo? = what day is it?). Bare 뭐 (mwo) can't sit in front of a noun.
English juggles at/on/in for time; Korean uses 에 (e) for all of it: 월요일에 (woryoire = on Monday). One particle covers the whole set.
에 (e) does two jobs in one sentence: time in 아침에 (achime = in the morning) and destination in 학교에 가요 (hakgyo-e gayo = go to school).
와요 (wayo) = motion toward the speaker, 가요 (gayo) = away. From your point of view a friend visiting you comes: 집에 와요 (jib-e wayo).
Two particles split the work: 월요일에 (woryoire) marks when, 회사에서 (hoesa-eseo) marks where the action happens – 에서 (eseo) for doing, 에 (e) for time.
같이 (gachi = together) looks like it should read ga-ti, but the t softens to ch before that i – say gachi.
Korean asks 'where is X' through the exist verb: 화장실이 어디에 있어요? (hwajangsil-i eodi-e isseoyo?) is literally 'bathroom where exists?'
Korean splits 'there' in two: 여기 (yeogi = here), 거기 (geogi = there by you), 저기 (jeogi = over there). 여기에 있어요 (yeogi-e isseoyo) = it's here.
Location words follow their noun: 학교 옆에 (hakgyo yeop-e) is literally 'school beside-at' – the reverse of English 'next to the school'.
Just being somewhere takes 에 (e): 집에 있어요 (jib-e isseoyo = is at home). Save 에서 (eseo) for places where an action happens.
너무 (neomu) is literally 'too (much)', but everyday speech also uses it for plain 'so': 너무 비싸요 (neomu bissayo) can be a real complaint or just emphasis.
아침 (achim) means both morning and breakfast: 아침을 먹다 (achimeul meokda) is literally 'eat the morning'. Context decides which one you mean.
Adverbs sit right before the verb: 늦게 일어났어요 (neutge ireonasseoyo) is literally 'late got-up' – English tacks 'late' on at the end instead.
The loanword 치킨 (chikin) narrowed to fried chicken only – chicken as meat in cooking is 닭고기 (dakgogi).
푹 (puk) is the go-to intensifier for rest and sleep: 푹 쉴 거예요 (puk swil geoyeyo) = rest up properly; 푹 자요 (puk jayo) = sleep soundly.
내년에 (naenyeone = next year) keeps its 에 (e), but 오늘, 내일, 어제 (oneul, naeil, eoje = today, tomorrow, yesterday) drop it – the everyday trio goes bare.
새 (sae = new) only works in front of a noun: 새 프로젝트 (sae peurojekteu). To say something IS new you need the verb form 새로워요 (saerowoyo).
The word after 너무 (neomu) sets the tone: with 짜요 (jjayo = salty) it's a genuine 'too salty' complaint; before praise it would just mean 'so'.
까지 (kkaji) stretches from 'up to' into 'even': 국물까지 (gungmulkkaji) = even the broth – all the way down the list to the last thing.
돼요? (dwaeyo? = does it work?) is the all-purpose 'can I / do you take': 카드 돼요? (kadeu dwaeyo?) covers 'do you take cards?' in two words.
The -(으)ㄹ게요 (-lgeyo) ending offers an action to the listener: 제가 계산할게요 (jega gyesanhalgeyo) = I'll get the bill – a volunteer move, not a prediction.
고기를 구웠어요 (gogireul guwosseoyo = grilled meat) – at a Korean barbecue the grill is set into your table and you cook the meat yourselves.
갈아타요 (garatayo = transfer) splits into 갈아 (gara = change) + 타다 (tada = ride) – literally 'change-ride', which is exactly what a transfer is.
보다 (boda) after a noun means 'than': 버스보다 빨라요 (beoseuboda ppallayo = faster than the bus). The thing you compare against carries the marker, not the subject.
내릴게요 (naerilgeyo) uses -(으)ㄹ게요 (-lgeyo) to flag an action the listener should know about – you're telling the driver you're getting off, not predicting it.
달 (dal) means both moon and month – 다음 달 (daeum dal = next month) is literally 'next moon', a leftover from moon-based months.
에서 (eseo) and 까지 (kkaji) bracket a route as 'from...to': 서울에서 부산까지 (seoureseo busankkaji = from Seoul to Busan).
Clock time mixes both number systems: hours take native numbers – 두 시 (du si = two o'clock) – while minutes switch to Sino-Korean with 분 (bun).
이제 (ije) is 'now' with a before/after edge – something changed: 이제 알아요 (ije arayo) = now I know, I didn't before. Plain 'right now' is 지금 (jigeum).
보다 (boda = than) attaches to abstract nouns too: 생각보다 (saenggakboda) is literally 'than thought' – the everyday way to say 'than I expected'.
한테 (hante) marks a person on the receiving end: 가족한테 보냈어요 (gajokhante bonaesseoyo = sent to my family). Places take 에 (e) instead.
못 (mot = can't) goes right before the verb: 못 잊어요 (mot ijeoyo = can't forget). It marks inability – 안 (an) would mean you simply don't.
English says a place is crowded; Korean says the people are many: 사람이 많아요 (saram-i manayo). The crowd is the subject, not the store.
No -er endings in Korean – comparatives just add 더 (deo = more) before the word: 더 쌌어요 (deo ssasseoyo) = was cheaper, literally 'more was-cheap'.
English puts 'new' on the glasses; Korean puts it on the buying: 새로 샀어요 (saero sasseoyo = newly bought) – the adverb carries what the adjective would.
로 (ro) also marks a role: 선물로 (seonmullo = as a present) – the same particle that covers transport and direction stretches to 'in the capacity of'.
맞아요 (majayo) spans 'it fits' and 'that's right': 사이즈가 맞아요 (saijeu-ga majayo = the size fits) uses the same word you'd use to agree with someone.
